brief.topic: Why Learning Can Get Worse When Steps Get Bigger

s01: A learning algorithm can point downhill and still move further from the answer.
The direction is only half the story.
Here is a tiny model with one adjustable number.
Its loss is that number squared.
Zero is the best answer.
At any position, the slope is twice the number.
Gradient descent subtracts a step size times that slope.
Start at two.
With a step size of one quarter, the next number is one.
Then one half.
Each update halves the distance to zero.
Now use a step size of three quarters.
Two becomes minus one, then one half.
The point crosses the valley, but the jumps still shrink.
Crossing the answer is not automatically a failure.
With a step size of one, two becomes minus two, then two again.
The algorithm never settles.
Make the step even larger, and the jumps grow.
The direction still came from the slope.
The distance ruined the improvement.
For this particular loss, each update multiplies the number by one minus twice the step size.
We need that multiplier between minus one and one.
So a positive step smaller than one converges here.
Real models have different curvature; this threshold belongs to this bowl.

scenes.narration:
A learning algorithm can point downhill and still move further from the answer. The direction is only half the story.

Here is a tiny model with one adjustable number. Its loss is that number squared. Zero is the best answer. At any position, the slope is twice the number.

Gradient descent subtracts a step size times that slope. Start at two. With a step size of one quarter, the next number is one. Then one half. Each update halves the distance to zero.

Now use a step size of three quarters. Two becomes minus one, then one half. The point crosses the valley, but the jumps still shrink. Crossing the answer is not automatically a failure.

With a step size of one, two becomes minus two, then two again. The algorithm never settles.

Make the step even larger, and the jumps grow. The direction still came from the slope. The distance ruined the improvement.

For this particular loss, each update multiplies the number by one minus twice the step size. We need that multiplier between minus one and one. So a positive step smaller than one converges here. Real models have different curvature; this threshold belongs to this bowl.
